mium binding and release. Cr3þ has a d3 electron conﬁguration in its normal octahedral or pseudo-octahedral coordination envi-
ronment. This makes exchange of ligands at the metal center slow compared to those of most other ﬁrst row transition metal ions.
Transferrin binds chromium concomitantly with an equivalent of (bi)carbonate, making the binding of chromium ﬁrst order in the
concentration of bicarbonate; in the presence of approximately 25 mM bicarbonate (as in the bloodstream), Cr3þ binds tightly to
transferrin in minutes. In the absence of added bicarbonate, loading of transferrin with Cr3þ requires up to two weeks. Whether Cr3þ
loss from transferrin is fast enough to be physiologically relevant as been a question. Transferrin delivers metal ions to cells via
endocytosis. While release of Cr3þ from transferrin is slow, Cr3þ is rapidly released at the pH of endosomes (pH  5.5) from
the transferrin/transferrin receptor complex (Edwards et al., 2020). How Cr3þ moves from the endosome to the rest of the cell is
unknown; however, a recent study has shown at pH 5.5 that LMWCr binds Cr3þ 250-fold faster in the presence transferrin/trans-
ferrin receptor complex, making the peptide a candidate for the carrier of Cr3þ across the endosomal membrane.
